voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the Son of God, truly born of Mary, from the line of David - a real man who truly ate and drank, was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died. Not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father. He is the one through whom we give thanks. When we break bread together, we call the cup the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus.

Ignatius calls him our God again and again - in how he opens his letters, and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

Here is Ignatius himself: So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ was from the line of David. He was the son of Mary. He was truly born. He ate, and he drank. Under Pontius Pilate he was truly persecuted. He was truly crucified, and he died - while those in heaven and on earth and under the earth looked on. And he was truly raised from the dead when his Father raised him up. In the same way, his Father will raise us up too, all of us who believe in him, in Christ Jesus - apart from whom we have no true life.

voice_event.text:
He preached the Gospel that the apostles then handed on to us. He appointed the apostles, and they in turn appointed others to carry it forward after them. That is the chain by which it reached us - not by our own seeing, but by receiving what was handed down.

As for what he did in his own life - he ate and drank among people. He stood before Pilate. He was nailed to the cross and died there. Then the Father raised him from the dead. Those are the acts we return to again and again, because they are what make him real to us - truly human, truly killed, truly raised.

We should say plainly: none of us saw him ourselves. We have no stories of particular days with him, no memory of his voice or his hands at work. What we have is what the apostles wrote down and what they preached, read aloud in our gatherings. The memoirs they left, and the prophets' words that pointed toward him long before he came - that is how we know him.

results.message: What does the Two Ways mean?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
The Two Ways is the teaching given before the water. It opens with this: a way of life and a way of death lie before every person, and there is a great difference between them. The way of life is loving God who made you, and loving your neighbor as yourself. And whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to another. That choice between the two roads is not made once and settled. It is kept daily.

In at least one of our own communities, this is what a new member was taught - not the harder stories from the older scriptures, but this direct instruction. Two ways lie open, love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way. This comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached.

Here is how that manual itself opens: There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
We believed the Two Ways because it was handed down to us as the shape of what it means to choose life. Before the water, a person preparing for baptism was taught that two ways lay open - a way of life and a way of death - and that which one a person walked was a live, continuing choice, not a nature settled once and for all. This teaching was inherited as a tool for shaping a new member, adaptable to a community's own occasion rather than issued from a single central authority.

The logic behind it is this: we were not teaching that a person becomes something fixed at baptism and then simply is that thing forever. We were teaching that the road you walk is chosen daily. Love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you - those are not ideas to agree with once. They are a road to keep walking.

The teaching itself circulated wider than any one community's own book. It appears in more than one form, in more than one place. That tells us it was recognized as a fitting way to form someone new to the assembly, even though we cannot say every household among us used it.

Here is the opening of the manual itself: There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
We will give you Hermas, a freedman in Rome. He reports a series of visions, delivered through an elderly woman who turns out to be the Church herself. Their message: God has granted one further chance to repent after baptism, before that door closes. That is the shape of his life as we have it - not a biography of all his days, but a man wrestling with the question of whether repentance is still open after the water, and being told it is, once more, but not forever.

Hermas himself was taught plainly: put doubting away from yourself. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one.

Here is what the Shepherd told Hermas directly: Put doubting away from you, and do not hesitate to ask the Lord for anything, saying to yourself, How can I ask anything from the Lord and receive it, when I have sinned so greatly against him? Do not think this way. Instead, turn to the Lord with your whole heart, and ask from him without doubting, and you will know his great compassion - that he will never abandon you, but will fulfill the request of your soul.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
What you need to understand is this: the people whose voices you can actually hear from us are not the people who filled our rooms. Almost none of the people who actually gathered with us left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place.

And here is the second thing: we never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyterion - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

What held us together across that disagreement was the table. The thanksgiving - the eucharistia - the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. We returned to it again and again, to be formed once more into one body. Its order varied from household to household. But the table itself was constant.

Here is Justin describing what happened when his own community gathered: On the day called Sunday, everyone who lives in the cities or in the country gathers together in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read for as long as time allows. When the reader stops, the president speaks -- he instructs us, and urges us to imitate these good things.
